orders.description: Defendant's appeal from the August 29, 2014 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on black ice outside the main entrance of the building where she worked. Defendant's employee described salting an hour earlier and seeing no ice, while plaintiff described ice and no visible salt immediately after her fall.

legal_issues.finding: Noncreation was part of the initial burden. Conflicting submissions defeated the overall showing; the opinion does not separately find defendant created ice.
The initial burden included lack of actual notice. The overall showing failed, but the court did not separately establish actual knowledge.
The initial burden included lack of constructive notice. The employee's inspection/salting account and plaintiff's contrary observations did not establish entitlement to judgment.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant's employee affidavit described salting approximately one hour before the fall and observing no ice.
Defendant submitted plaintiff's deposition describing ice covering the entranceway and no observed salt after the fall.

quality.notes: The supplied opinion attributes the building to defendant and establishes employee salting, but does not expressly establish the exterior entrance area's private ownership/lease or boundary. Maintenance alone is not used to infer private property. No institutional/building subtype is inferred from the name. Employee means plaintiff worked at this building, not necessarily for defendant. Accident date is unstated. Conflicting ice/salt accounts are preserved without resolving credibility.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff commenced this action after she allegedly slipped and fell on black ice outside the main entrance of the defendant's building where she worked.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Kamins, J.), entered August 29, 2014, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

In support of its motion, the defendant submitted an affidavit from one of its employees stating that he spread rock salt in the area of the front entranceway to the building about an hour before the plaintiff's accident and had not observed any ice at that time.

However, the defendant also submitted the transcript of the deposition of the plaintiff, who testified that the main entranceway was covered with ice at the time of the accident and that she did not observe any rock salt on the ground immediately after she fell.
Under the circumstances presented here, the defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment, without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers

Thus, a defendant who moves for summary judgment in a slip-and-fall case has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the hazardous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it

orders.description: Defendants' appeal from the August 5, 2009 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped down interior stairs in defendants' building and described rainwater tracked from the lobby. She also advanced a wall-leak account and a theory involving separated metal stair nosing.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established lack of notice; plaintiff had not informed them and supplied no competent evidence raising a question of notice from another source.
General awareness of rainwater on the lobby/stairs did not establish notice of the specific condition causing the fall.
Plaintiff's repeated-rainwater account showed only general awareness; the new recurring-wall-leak account conflicted with her deposition and did not defeat summary judgment.
Plaintiff raised no triable issue on the alternate theory that separated metal nosing caused her slip; the opinion does not conclusively identify a different cause.
The asserted Administrative Code stair violation raised no triable issue; the opinion gives no additional technical analysis of that provision.
The opposing affidavit's new leak account conflicted with earlier deposition testimony and was insufficient to defeat the motion; substantive notice and alternate theories were also assessed.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's account of recurring rainwater and her later opposing affidavit were considered; the leak assertion conflicted with her deposition.

quality.notes: The source expressly establishes building ownership and management, without specifying use or plaintiff's role. Separate water, leak and metal-nosing theories remain allegations rather than established defects. No specific code breach or alternate cause is invented from the abbreviated rejection of those theories. Accident date is unstated.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Wilma Guzman, J.), entered August 5, 2009, which, in an action for personal injuries allegedly sustained in a slip and fall down interior stairs in a building owned and managed by defendants, denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, and the motion granted.

Defendants established their prima facie entitlement to summary judgment by submitting evidence that they lacked notice of the condition alleged to have caused plaintiffs fall. In opposition, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

Although she stated that water accumulated on the lobby floor in the building each time it rained and that the water would be tracked onto the interior stairs, this raised no more than a general awareness that the floor became wet during inclement weather, which is insufficient to establish constructive notice of the specific condition causing her injury
Plaintiff neither informed defendants of the alleged hazardous condition nor produced competent evidence to raise a factual question as to whether they had received notice from any other source

Furthermore, plaintiffs claim in her affidavit in opposition that a leak in the wall near the mailboxes resulted in a puddle of water at the bottom of the staircase each time it rained, is not consistent with her earlier deposition testimony and thus, insufficient to defeat defendants’ motion

Nor did plaintiff raise a triable issue of fact on her other theories of liability, including that the subject stairs were in violation of Administrative Code of City of NY § 27-375 (h) and that she was caused to fall by a piece of metal nosing that had separated from the stair on which she slipped.
The Clerk is directed to enter judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the December 22, 2009 defense judgment after the liability trial.
orders.trial_court_action: Entered judgment dismissing the complaint after a jury verdict for defendant on liability.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff alleged an ice-related fall in defendant's parking lot on March 2, 2005 and testified that she saw and felt ice. A former mechanic who arrived afterward testified that he recalled no ice; his 911 call and differing accounts of his recollection were disputed.

legal_issues.finding: The court upheld exclusion as a present sense impression about an accident not witnessed by the caller, but held the tape could refresh recollection and should have been admitted for the limited impeachment purpose after a proper foundation. Evidentiary errors required a new liability trial.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff testified that she saw and felt ice during her fall.
Former employee's trial/deposition accounts and memory of the scene were disputed; he had not witnessed the fall.

The 911 audio recording was rejected as substantive present-sense-impression evidence of how the fall occurred, but could refresh recollection and impeach the caller. It was not independently played or transcribed here.

quality.notes: Procedural-only exclusion: the analyzed appellate grounds concern hearsay, refreshed recollection and impeachment, not resolution of negligence/notice/defect merits. Admissibility for impeachment does not establish the truth of ice or causation. Full reversal with a new trial is retained rather than remand_only. The source calls the witness Brian Fina in P001 and Pina thereafter; quotations preserve this inconsistency and no identity correction is asserted. Private parking control is attributed through defendant's parking lot/property; associated business use and legal title are not inferred from the case name. Plaintiff's role is unknown.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the judgment is reversed, on the law, with costs, the complaint is reinstated, and a new trial on the issue of liability is granted.

The plaintiff alleges that, on March 2, 2005, she slipped and fell on ice in the defendant’s parking lot. She commenced this action against the defendant to recover damages for personal injuries, alleging that the defendant was liable because it negligently maintained its property.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from a judgment of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Sweeney, J.), entered December 22, 2009, which, upon a jury verdict on the issue of liability, is in favor of the defendant and against her dismissing the complaint.
On her direct case, the plaintiff testified that, as she fell, she saw and felt ice on the ground.
He recalled that, during that time, he looked around and “[t]o the best of [his] knowledge, there was no ice” on the ground.

Upon cross-examination by the defendant, his former employer, Pina went on to testify that he had not witnessed the accident. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the defendant on the issue of liability.

Here, Pina did not witness the accident, but arrived at the scene after the fall. Thus, contrary to the plaintiffs contention, any statements Pina may have made to the 911 operator about how the accident occurred were not present sense impressions of that issue, as he did not perceive the accident at all
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the plaintiffs request to admit the 911 tape into evidence under the present sense impression exception to the hearsay rule.

We agree with the plaintiff, however, that the Supreme Court should have allowed her to refresh Pina’s recollection with the 911 tape. At trial, Pina explained that he had no independent recollection of the incident. Such testimony was sufficient to allow the plaintiff to play the 911 tape outside the presence of the jury and allow Pina to refresh his recollection about what he had told the 911 operator

Upon the plaintiff’s laying of such foundation, the Supreme Court should have admitted the 911 tape into evidence as a prior inconsistent statement by Pina for the limited purpose of allowing the plaintiff to impeach his credibility

Accordingly, the judgment must be reversed, the complaint must be reinstated, and a new trial on the issue of liability must be conducted. In light of our determination, we need not reach the parties’ remaining contentions.
Before Pina testified, the plaintiff sought to admit into evidence a tape of Pina’s 911 call under the present sense impression or excited utterance exceptions to the hearsay rule.

After Pina gave this testimony, the plaintiff’s counsel requested a bench conference, after which counsel stated, on the record, that Pina had just testified that he had seen no ice on the ground immediately after the accident, but in his prior deposition testimony, he admitted telling the 911 operator that he had seen “ice on the ground that caused [plaintiff] to slip and fall.”

orders.description: Defendants' appeal from the November 20, 2019 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped on a rolled-up carpet inside defendants' store. The deposition record also described a preexisting bundled-up section of carpeted floor; the exact accident location and mechanism were disputed.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the reasonably-safe-premises duty; defendants initially established safe maintenance, but the complete deposition record raised triable issues.
Noncreation appears in the initial-burden rule; the application does not separately decide who created the carpet condition.
Actual notice appears in the initial-burden rule, while the application identifies a constructive-notice issue without separately resolving actual notice.
The complete deposition transcripts raised a triable issue of constructive notice of the alleged preexisting bundled-up carpeting.
Defendants' excerpts initially supported a speculative-cause showing, but complete transcripts raised factual questions about location and a trip on preexisting bundled-up carpeting.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants offered plaintiff's deposition excerpts; plaintiff submitted the complete transcript, which helped raise factual issues.
Store-manager deposition excerpts were submitted by defendants and the complete transcript by plaintiff.

quality.notes: Defendants met the initial burden, but opposition raised triable issues; do not report an initial defense failure or proven notice. The source changes from he to her; exact quotes preserve it without inferring demographics. The May 2017 date is commencement, not accident date. Rolled-up carpet and bundled-up carpeted floor are alternative source descriptions, not independently resolved. Plaintiff's role is unknown.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when he tripped and fell over a rolled-up carpet on the floor in a store owned and operated by the defendants.
The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendants submitted, inter alia, excerpts of the deposition testimony transcripts of the plaintiff and of their store manager, which demonstrated, prima facie, that they maintained their premises in a reasonably safe condition
and that the jury would have to speculate as to the cause of the plaintiff's fall

However, in opposition, the plaintiff, through the submission of the complete transcript of her deposition testimony and the complete deposition transcript of the defendants' store manager, raised triable issues of fact as to where the accident occurred, whether the plaintiff tripped and fell on a [*2] preexisting "bundled-up" section of the carpeted floor, and whether the defendants had constructive notice of such condition
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
A property owner has a duty to maintain its premises in a reasonably safe condition

"To demonstrate entitlement to summary judgment, an owner of real property must establish that it maintained the premises in a reasonably safe condition, and that it did not create a dangerous or defective condition on the property or have either actual or constructive notice of a dangerous or defective condition for a sufficient length of time to remedy it"

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the March 8, 2018 order refusing to vacate the earlier default summary-judgment order and deny the underlying motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied plaintiff's CPLR 5015(a) motion to vacate the February 2, 2017 unopposed summary-judgment order and thereupon deny defendant's motion.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, who lived at defendant's property, allegedly slipped on snow or ice on its exterior steps on March 3, 2015. Defendant presented a verbal daily-maintenance arrangement; plaintiff disputed being responsible for snow and ice removal.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant initially supported a verbal arrangement assigning maintenance to plaintiff, but his affidavit raised a triable issue whether he was responsible for snow/ice removal.
Plaintiff raised a triable issue whether the snow/ice had existed long enough to constitute constructive notice; notice was not conclusively found.

The approximately seven-day opposition delay, absence of willfulness/prejudice and law-office error justified vacating the default. The court then substantively found triable maintenance-responsibility and notice issues.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's opposing affidavit disputed snow-removal responsibility and described not performing it for decades.
Defendant offered evidence of a verbal maintenance agreement; the opinion does not specify the form of that proof.

quality.notes: Not default-only: P005–P006 expressly determine the underlying negligence motion's merits. One independently appealed March 8, 2018 order; vacatur of the earlier default order is consequential relief, not a second appealed disposition or mixed outcome. Plaintiff is explicitly resident but not explicitly tenant, employee or contractor, so injured_role is other. Verbal maintenance responsibility remains disputed. All findings are draft interpretations under unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order entered March 8, 2018, is reversed, on the law, on the facts, and in the exercise of discretion, with costs, the plaintiff's motion, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) to vacate the order entered February 2, 2017, and thereupon to deny the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted, the order entered February 2, 2017, is vacated, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.
On March 3, 2015, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell on snow and/or ice on the exterior steps of certain property owned by the defendant.

The order denied the plaintiff's motion, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) to vacate an order of the same court entered February 2, 2017, granting the defendant's unopposed motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, and thereupon to deny the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Thereafter, the plaintiff moved, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) to vacate the order entered February 2, 2017, and thereupon, to deny the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, asserting, inter alia, that the deadline to serve opposition papers to the defendant's motion for summary judgment had been mis-diaried by counsel.

Here, given the totality of all relevant factors, including the delay of only approximately seven days from the due date for opposition papers to the time the plaintiff served opposition papers, the lack of any evidence of willfulness by the plaintiff, or prejudice to the defendant from the delay, and the strong public policy in favor of resolving cases on the merits, the Supreme Court improvidently exercised its discretion in not accepting the plaintiff's excuse of law office failure

With regard to the merits of the defendant's motion for summary judgment, the defendant established her prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by presenting evidence that the plaintiff, who lived at the premises, had a verbal agreement to perform daily maintenance of the property, including taking care of snow and ice conditions on the premises

However, in opposition to the defendant's prima facie showing, the plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact as to whether he was responsible for snow and ice removal, by submitting his affidavit, wherein he averred that he had not been involved in snow and ice removal for decades, which he was physically unable to perform.

Moreover, the plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact as to whether the snow and/or ice condition was present for a sufficient length of time before the accident so as to constitute constructive notice of the condition

Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the plaintiff's motion, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) to vacate the order entered February 2, 2017, and thereupon denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
